questions.question: A 68-year-old ICU patient on mechanical ventilation for 5 days develops a new fever of 39.0 C, purulent tracheal secretions, and a new infiltrate on chest X-ray. Which evidence-based nursing bundle interventions specifically prevent this Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP)? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Elevating the head of the bed to 30–45 degrees unless contraindicated
Performing regular oral care with chlorhexidine solution per protocol
Daily sedation vacations and readiness-to-wean assessments
Routine prophylactic replacement of ventilator circuits every 24 hours

questions.explanation: The IHI/CDC VAP prevention bundle includes HOB elevation 30–45 degrees, daily sedation interruption/spontaneous breathing trials, peptic ulcer and DVT prophylaxis, and oral care with chlorhexidine. Routine daily circuit changes actually INCREASE VAP risk by introducing condensation/contamination; circuits are changed only when visibly soiled or malfunctioning.
questions.hint: Select the three proven VAP-bundle steps and avoid the outdated practice that actually raises contamination risk.
questions.subject: Infection Control & Isolation

questions.question: A nurse is inserting a central venous catheter (CVC) assisting a physician. Which actions belong to the Central Line-Associated Bloodstream Infection (CLABSI) insertion bundle? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Performing skin antisepsis with > 0.5% chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% alcohol and allowing it to dry completely
Using maximal sterile barrier precautions (cap, mask, sterile gown, sterile gloves, full-body sterile drape)
Avoiding the femoral vein site in adult patients whenever possible due to higher infection risk
Applying topical antibiotic ointment routinely to all non-dialysis central line sites

questions.explanation: CLABSI prevention requires hand hygiene, maximal sterile barrier precautions, > 0.5% chlorhexidine-alcohol skin prep, optimal site selection (avoiding femoral in adults), and daily line-necessity review. Routine topical antibiotic ointment on non-dialysis CVCs promotes fungal/resistant colonization.
questions.hint: Focus on maximal sterile barriers, preferred antisepsis, and anatomical site safety in adults.
questions.subject: Infection Control & Isolation

questions.question: A patient admitted to the ward has a draining stage-3 sacral pressure ulcer positive for Vancomycin-Resistant Enterococci (VRE). Which dedicated equipment policy should the nurse enforce under Contact Precautions?

options.text: Share the ward's rolling vital signs monitor without wiping between rooms
Use dedicated non-critical patient care equipment (stethoscope, BP cuff, thermometer) kept in the room, or thoroughly disinfect before use on another patient
Autoclave the electronic blood pressure machine after every reading
Place the patient in a negative-pressure AIIR room

questions.explanation: Under Contact Precautions (MRSA, VRE, C. diff, scabies, RSV), dedicated non-critical equipment (or single-use disposables) prevents indirect fomite transmission. If sharing is unavoidable, thorough disinfection with an EPA-approved agent is mandatory before reuse.
questions.hint: Think about how shared ward stethoscopes or cuffs spread multi-drug-resistant bacteria between beds.
questions.subject: Infection Control & Isolation

questions.question: Within how many hours of a high-risk HIV needle-stick exposure should Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) antiretroviral therapy ideally be initiated, and what is the maximum window beyond which PEP is generally not recommended?

options.text: Ideally within 24 hours; maximum 7 days
Ideally within 2 hours; maximum 72 hours (3 days), continued for 28 days
Ideally within 12 hours; maximum 14 days
Only after the healthcare worker tests HIV-positive at 6 weeks

questions.explanation: [AIIMS NORCET / NACO PYQ] NACO and CDC guidelines state that HIV PEP is most effective when started within 2 hours of exposure, should NOT be initiated after 72 hours, and is taken for a full 28-day course.
questions.hint: Recall the urgent 2-hour ideal start, the 3-day cutoff, and the 4-week treatment duration.
questions.subject: Infection Control & Isolation

questions.question: A nurse is preparing a patient's abdomen for an elective laparotomy. According to WHO Surgical Site Infection (SSI) prevention guidelines, how should hair at the surgical site be managed if removal is strictly necessary?

options.text: Shave closely with a dry disposable razor the night before surgery
Do not remove hair unless it interferes with the incision; if necessary, trim using electric clippers immediately before surgery
Apply depilatory wax 48 hours prior to surgery
Shave with a straight blade inside the operating theater

questions.explanation: Razor shaving creates microscopic skin abrasions that rapidly colonize with bacteria and increase SSI rates. WHO guidelines recommend leaving hair intact or using electric clippers (never razors) right before the operation.
questions.hint: Consider which hair-removal method avoids creating microscopic skin cuts that harbor bacteria.
questions.subject: Infection Control & Isolation

questions.question: A patient in the emergency room is suspected of having Ebola virus disease / viral hemorrhagic fever with vomiting and diarrhea. Which isolation tier is required?

options.text: Standard precautions only
Droplet precautions only
Strict Contact + Droplet/Airborne precautions (fluid-impermeable full-body PPE, double gloves, face shield/N95, single isolation room)
Protective positive-pressure isolation

questions.explanation: Viral hemorrhagic fevers (Ebola, Marburg) have extreme mortality and spread via direct contact with blood/body fluids and aerosol-generating procedures, requiring strict isolation with impermeable full-body PPE and no exposed skin.
questions.hint: Choose the highest-tier barrier combination that prevents any skin or mucosal exposure to infectious body fluids.
questions.subject: Infection Control & Isolation

questions.question: Two patients on a pediatric ward both have confirmed Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) bronchiolitis, and no single rooms remain available. What is the acceptable infection control practice?

options.text: Place an RSV patient in a shared room with a child recovering from an appendectomy
Cohort the two patients with the same confirmed pathogen (RSV) together, maintaining >= 3 feet separation and curtains drawn
Place both children in the hallway
Cancel Contact precautions because they share a room

questions.explanation: Cohorting allows patients infected with the EXACT same confirmed organism (and no other co-infections) to share a room when single rooms are unavailable, while staff still change PPE and perform hand hygiene between the two patients.
questions.hint: Recall the infection-control term for grouping patients who have the identical confirmed pathogen.
questions.subject: Infection Control & Isolation

questions.question: A patient with active varicella (chickenpox) is admitted to an isolation room. When can Airborne and Contact precautions be safely discontinued?

options.text: 24 hours after starting oral acyclovir
As soon as the fever resolves
Only when ALL vesicular skin lesions have dried and crusted over
After 3 days of hospitalization regardless of rash status

questions.explanation: Varicella remains contagious via both airborne aerosols and direct contact with vesicular fluid until every single lesion has completely crusted/scabbed over (typically 5–7 days after rash onset).
questions.hint: Focus on the physical stage of the skin blisters that signals viral shedding has stopped.
questions.subject: Infection Control & Isolation

questions.question: Which stage of the infectious process is characterized by vague, non-specific symptoms such as malaise, low-grade fever, and fatigue, during which the patient is often MOST contagious to others?

options.text: Incubation period
Prodromal stage
Illness stage
Convalescence stage

questions.explanation: The four stages of infection are Incubation (entry to first symptom), Prodromal (non-specific early symptoms—high contagiousness because the patient may not yet know they are sick), Illness (specific localized/systemic signs), and Convalescence (recovery).
questions.hint: Identify the early stage of vague malaise right before full-blown disease-specific signs appear.
questions.subject: Infection Control & Isolation

questions.question: A nurse opens a sterile bottle of normal saline to pour into a sterile basin on a sterile dressing tray. Which technique maintains surgical asepsis?

options.text: Place the bottle cap face-down on the bedside table
Touch the rim of the bottle directly to the edge of the sterile basin to prevent splashing
Hold the bottle 4–6 inches above the basin with the label facing the palm, pour smoothly without splashing, and place the cap face-up on a clean surface
Pour from a height of 18 inches to stay far from the field

questions.explanation: Keeping the label in the palm prevents drips from staining it; pouring from 4–6 inches avoids both direct lip-to-basin contact and splashing (which causes strike-through contamination); caps are placed face-up so the inner sterile rim never touches an unsterile table.
questions.hint: Think about avoiding both direct lip touch and fluid splashing while protecting the inside of the bottle cap.
questions.subject: Infection Control & Isolation

questions.question: Which of the following infections is caused by an ENDOGENOUS source of Healthcare-Associated Infection (HAI)?

options.text: A surgical patient acquires MRSA from a nurse's unwashed hands
A patient receiving broad-spectrum IV antibiotics develops overgrowth of their own intestinal Clostridioides difficile or oral Candida albicans
A burn patient acquires Pseudomonas from contaminated hydrotherapy tank water
A newborn acquires RSV from a visitor with a cold

questions.explanation: Endogenous HAIs arise from the patient's own normal flora shifting to a sterile site or overgrowing when host defenses or normal microbiota are disrupted (e.g., antibiotic-associated C. diff or candidiasis). Exogenous HAIs come from external sources (staff, visitors, equipment).
questions.hint: Separate infections arising from the patient's own body flora from those introduced from outside.
questions.subject: Infection Control & Isolation

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a patient with an indwelling Foley catheter. Which nursing practice is a DIRECT breach of CAUTI prevention guidelines?

options.text: Securing the catheter tubing to the patient's thigh to prevent urethral traction
Keeping the drainage bag below bladder level and off the floor
Lifting the drainage bag above bladder level while transferring the patient onto a stretcher
Emptying the drainage bag using a separate clean measuring container per patient

questions.explanation: Elevating the drainage bag above bladder level causes retrograde reflux of contaminated urine back into the sterile bladder, sharply increasing CAUTI risk.
questions.hint: Watch for the action that lets urine flow backward by gravity into the bladder.
questions.subject: Infection Control & Isolation

questions.question: A patient with suspected meningococcal meningitis starts IV ceftriaxone at 10:00 AM. After how many hours of effective antimicrobial therapy can Droplet precautions typically be discontinued?

options.text: Immediately after the first IV dose finishes
After 24 hours of effective antibiotic therapy
After 7 days of therapy
Only after a repeat lumbar puncture at 14 days

questions.explanation: For Neisseria meningitidis (and Haemophilus influenzae type b), patients generally become non-infectious and Droplet precautions can be lifted after 24 hours of effective antimicrobial therapy.
questions.hint: Recall the standard 1-day effective-antibiotic duration for meningococcal droplet isolation.
questions.subject: Infection Control & Isolation

questions.question: Which airborne isolation room parameter is monitored daily outside an AIIR housing an active TB patient to confirm negative pressure?

options.text: Room humidity at 90%
Pressure differential gauge (manometer/magnehelic gauge) showing inward airflow from corridor into the room (and visual smoke/tissue test)
Positive outward airflow into the nursing station
Keeping the room door propped open by 6 inches

questions.explanation: Negative pressure means air flows INWARD from the clean hallway into the isolation room (and is exhausted outside via HEPA filtration), verified daily via a magnehelic pressure gauge or flutter strip while keeping the door tightly closed.
questions.hint: Check which airflow direction keeps contaminated room air from escaping into the hallway.
questions.subject: Infection Control & Isolation

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a patient with scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei) infestation. Which isolation precaution is required until 24 hours after effective topical permethrin treatment?

options.text: Airborne precautions
Droplet precautions
Contact precautions
Protective isolation

questions.explanation: Scabies spreads via prolonged skin-to-skin contact and contaminated bedding/clothing, requiring Contact precautions (gown, gloves, bagged linen washing in hot water) until 24 hours after effective scabicidal therapy.
questions.hint: Consider how mites spread from skin or bedding to caregivers.
questions.subject: Infection Control & Isolation

questions.question: Which statement BEST distinguishes Medical Asepsis (Clean Technique) from Surgical Asepsis (Sterile Technique)?

options.text: Medical asepsis eliminates all microorganisms including bacterial spores; surgical asepsis only reduces them
Medical asepsis reduces the number and spread of microorganisms; surgical asepsis eliminates ALL microorganisms and spores from an area or object
Surgical asepsis is used for oral medication administration
Medical asepsis requires sterile gloves for all procedures

questions.explanation: Medical asepsis (clean technique—hand hygiene, clean gloves, routine surface cleaning) limits the growth and transmission of microbes. Surgical asepsis (sterile technique—OT, catheterization, central lines) eliminates 100% of microbes and spores.
questions.hint: Contrast "reducing microbial transfer" with "eliminating every single microbe and spore."
questions.subject: Infection Control & Isolation

questions.question: A nurse is educating a neutropenic chemotherapy patient's family before they visit the positive-pressure room. Which visitor instruction is MOST critical?

options.text: Bring freshly cut roses to brighten the room
Visitors with any cold, cough, fever, or recent live-virus vaccination must not visit, and all healthy visitors must perform strict hand hygiene
Bring homemade unpasteurized yogurt and raw salads
Share the patient's drinking glass to encourage fluid intake

questions.explanation: Severely neutropenic patients lack neutrophils to fight even mild environmental or viral pathogens. Sick visitors, fresh flowers/soil, and raw unpeeled foods pose severe opportunistic infection risks.
questions.hint: Identify the rule that keeps infectious visitors and microbial sources away from an immunocompromised host.
questions.subject: Infection Control & Isolation

questions.question: A nurse receives a splash of a patient's blood directly into their eyes during an emergency arterial blood gas draw because goggles were not worn. What is the nurse's IMMEDIATE action?

options.text: Rub both eyes with a dry sterile gauze
Irrigate both eyes immediately with copious clean running water or normal saline at an eyewash station for at least 15 minutes, then report for PEP
Instill alcohol-based eye drops
Wait until the end of the shift to notify occupational health

questions.explanation: Mucous membrane blood exposure (eyes/mouth) requires immediate, copious flushing with water or normal saline (15 minutes at an eyewash station) without rubbing, followed by prompt occupational exposure reporting and PEP assessment.
questions.hint: Recall the universal emergency first aid for any infectious splash into ocular mucous membranes.
questions.subject: Infection Control & Isolation

questions.question: Which of the following pathogens is transmitted primarily via the DROPLET route rather than the Airborne route?

options.text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Rubeola (Measles) virus
Bordetella pertussis
Varicella-zoster virus

questions.explanation: Bordetella pertussis (whooping cough) spreads via large respiratory droplets (> 5 microns) and requires Droplet precautions. TB, Measles, and Varicella require Airborne precautions.
questions.hint: Eliminate the three classic "MTV" airborne pathogens to find the droplet-borne infection.
questions.subject: Infection Control & Isolation

questions.question: In an outbreak investigation on a surgical ward, the infection control nurse calculates the Surgical Site Infection (SSI) rate. Under CDC NHSN criteria, a superficial incisional SSI occurs within how many days after an operative procedure?

options.text: 48 hours
7 days
30 days (and up to 90 days for certain deep/organ-space procedures involving implants)
1 year for all surgeries

questions.explanation: CDC NHSN defines superficial incisional SSI as occurring within 30 days post-operation (while deep incisional or organ/space SSIs involving specific implants are surveilled up to 90 days).
questions.hint: Recall the standard one-month post-op surveillance window for superficial wound infections.
questions.subject: Infection Control & Isolation

questions.question: A nurse enters a patient's room, shakes the patient's hand, adjusts the blanket, checks the radial pulse, and then prepares to perform a sterile tracheostomy suctioning. How many distinct WHO Hand Hygiene Moments occurred up to the start of suctioning?

options.text: One (only before entering the room)
Two (Moment 1 before touching the patient, and Moment 2 before the clean/aseptic suctioning procedure)
Zero, because sterile gloves will be worn for suctioning
Four

questions.explanation: Even within the same patient encounter, transitioning from general patient contact (pulse/blanket = Moment 1) to an invasive aseptic task (tracheostomy suctioning = Moment 2) requires a SECOND hand hygiene action immediately before the aseptic procedure.
questions.hint: Count both the initial patient-contact trigger and the transition to an invasive airway task.
questions.subject: Hand Hygiene (WHO Standard)

questions.question: Why does the WHO recommend Alcohol-Based Hand Rub (ABHR) as the preferred gold-standard method for routine clinical hand antisepsis when hands are NOT visibly soiled? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Faster action (20–30 seconds vs 40–60 seconds for soap and water)
Superior broad-spectrum reduction of vegetative bacteria and enveloped viruses compared to plain soap
Better skin tolerability (contains emollients like glycerol) and higher staff compliance at point of care
Complete sporicidal destruction of Clostridioides difficile spores

questions.explanation: ABHR is faster, more microbicidal against vegetative bacteria/viruses, gentler on skin due to emollients, and accessible right at the bedside—boosting compliance. However, alcohol is NOT sporicidal against C. difficile.
questions.hint: Pick the three true clinical advantages of alcohol hand rub and exclude the claim about bacterial spores.
questions.subject: Hand Hygiene (WHO Standard)

questions.question: According to the WHO formulation for local production of Alcohol-Based Hand Rub, which three main active/functional ingredients are combined (along with sterile distilled/boiled cold water)?

options.text: Methanol, bleach, and fragrance
Ethanol (80% v/v) or Isopropyl alcohol (75% v/v), Hydrogen peroxide (0.125% v/v), and Glycerol (1.45% v/v)
Phenol, iodine, and mineral oil
Chlorhexidine, acetone, and paraffin

questions.explanation: WHO local ABHR formulations use Ethanol 80% (or Isopropanol 75%) as the antimicrobial agent, Hydrogen peroxide 0.125% to inactivate contaminating bacterial spores in the bulk bottle (not as an active hand antiseptic), and Glycerol 1.45% as a humectant/emollient to protect skin.
questions.hint: Look for the combination containing alcohol, a trace peroxide stabilizer, and a skin-protecting humectant.
questions.subject: Hand Hygiene (WHO Standard)

questions.question: A nurse washes their hands with soap and water, rinses thoroughly, and reaches for an electric hot-air hand dryer versus single-use disposable paper towels in a clinical ICU. Which drying method is preferred by WHO infection control guidelines?

options.text: Shared cloth roller towel
Single-use disposable paper towels (patting dry gently without harsh rubbing)
Wiping hands on a clean nurse uniform
Leaving hands dripping wet to air-dry inside gloves

questions.explanation: Single-use disposable paper towels dry hands rapidly, mechanically remove residual bacteria, avoid aerosolizing microbes (unlike jet air dryers), and can be used to turn off manual faucets without recontaminating hands.
questions.hint: Choose the single-use drying method that avoids microbial aerosols and lets you close a manual faucet safely.
questions.subject: Hand Hygiene (WHO Standard)

questions.question: Which step in the WHO 6-step hand hygiene technique cleans the spaces BETWEEN the fingers from the palmar side?

options.text: Step 1: Rub hands palm to palm
Step 3: Palm to palm with fingers interlaced
Step 5: Rotational rubbing of thumbs
Step 6: Rotational rubbing of fingertips in opposing palm

questions.explanation: Step 1 = palm to palm; Step 2 = right palm over left dorsum with interlaced fingers (and vice versa); Step 3 = palm to palm with fingers interlaced; Step 4 = backs of fingers to opposing palms interlocked; Step 5 = rotational thumb rubbing; Step 6 = fingertips clasped in opposite palm.
questions.hint: Visualize pressing both palms together with your fingers woven between each other.
questions.subject: Hand Hygiene (WHO Standard)

questions.question: During a busy shift, a nurse applies alcohol-based hand rub and immediately pulls on nitrile gloves while the hands are still visibly wet with alcohol. What risks does this create? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Increased risk of skin irritation and irritant contact dermatitis under occlusive gloves
Potential degradation or micro-perforation of certain glove materials
Reduced antimicrobial contact time if alcohol is wiped off prematurely
Improved sterile barrier strength

questions.explanation: WHO explicitly mandates rubbing ABHR until hands are completely dry (20–30 sec) before donning gloves. Trapping wet alcohol inside gloves causes dermatitis, makes donning difficult, and can weaken glove integrity.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to both skin and glove material when wet alcohol is trapped inside tight gloves.
questions.subject: Hand Hygiene (WHO Standard)

questions.question: A nurse finishes emptying a Hemovac surgical drain (wearing clean gloves), removes the gloves, and immediately moves to document on the bedside computer without touching the patient again. Which WHO Moment for Hand Hygiene was required right after glove removal?

options.text: Moment 1: Before touching a patient
Moment 2: Before a clean/aseptic procedure
Moment 3: After body fluid exposure risk
Moment 5: After touching patient surroundings

questions.explanation: Emptying a bloody surgical drain creates direct body fluid exposure risk. Even though gloves were worn, Moment 3 (After body fluid exposure risk) mandates immediate hand hygiene upon removing gloves to protect both the nurse and the healthcare environment.
questions.hint: Match handling blood or surgical drainage directly to the specific WHO Moment designed for body fluids.
questions.subject: Hand Hygiene (WHO Standard)

questions.question: What is the difference between "Transient skin flora" and "Resident skin flora" on a healthcare worker's hands?

options.text: Resident flora is easily removed by plain soap; transient flora is impossible to remove

Transient flora colonizes superficial skin layers from patient/environment contact and is easily removed by routine hand hygiene; resident flora lives in deeper skin layers and requires antimicrobial agents (like surgical scrub) to reduce
Transient flora never causes healthcare-associated infections
Resident flora consists exclusively of MRSA and VRE

questions.explanation: Transient flora (e.g., MRSA, E. coli, Pseudomonas) is picked up on superficial skin during care, is the main cause of HAIs, and is readily removed by ABHR or soap. Resident flora (e.g., coagulase-negative staphylococci) resides in deeper epidermal layers/hair follicles and is reduced during surgical hand antisepsis.
questions.hint: Distinguish superficial "visiting" germs picked up from patients from deeper normal skin inhabitants.
questions.subject: Hand Hygiene (WHO Standard)

questions.question: A nurse is teaching a nursing student about the role of plain (non-antimicrobial) soap versus antimicrobial soap during handwashing. How does plain soap primarily clean hands?

options.text: By chemically destroying bacterial DNA and spores
By mechanical emulsification and suspension of dirt, lipids, and transient microbes so running water flushes them away
By leaving a 6-hour persistent bactericidal film on skin
By coagulating skin proteins

questions.explanation: Plain soap acts as a surfactant that lifts dirt, organic soil, and loosely attached transient microbes via friction so running water rinses them off; it has minimal intrinsic bactericidal activity.
questions.hint: Focus on physical lifting and rinsing away debris rather than chemical killing.
questions.subject: Hand Hygiene (WHO Standard)

questions.question: Which antimicrobial hand-scrub agent is noted for having the LONGEST persistent (residual) antimicrobial activity on skin after surgical hand preparation?

options.text: Plain bar soap
70% Ethyl alcohol alone
Chlorhexidine gluconate (2%–4% CHG)
Hydrogen peroxide 3%

questions.explanation: While alcohol provides the fastest immediate microbial kill, it has no residual effect once evaporated. Chlorhexidine gluconate (CHG) binds to the stratum corneum and provides prolonged residual antimicrobial activity lasting several hours.
questions.hint: Identify the surgical scrub agent famous for binding to skin and continuing to suppress bacteria for hours.
questions.subject: Hand Hygiene (WHO Standard)

questions.question: A nurse applies alcohol-based hand rub from a wall dispenser. Approximately how much volume of ABHR should be dispensed to ensure complete coverage of all hand surfaces for 20–30 seconds?

options.text: 0.5 mL (a few drops)
A palmful (approximately 3 mL, or 1–2 full pump depressions)
15 mL (one tablespoon)
30 mL

questions.explanation: WHO specifies applying a "palmful" (about 3 mL) sufficient to keep all surfaces of both hands wet throughout the full 20–30 seconds of friction. If hands dry in less than 15 seconds, insufficient product was applied.
questions.hint: Think of the volume needed so your hands stay moist across all six rubbing steps without drying too early.
questions.subject: Hand Hygiene (WHO Standard)

questions.question: A nurse notices a visitor leaving the room of a patient with C. difficile diarrhea and using the hallway alcohol hand rub dispenser instead of the sink. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Say nothing because alcohol rub is sufficient for visitors
Politely educate the visitor to wash their hands thoroughly with soap and water because alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores
Instruct the visitor to use double the amount of alcohol rub
Ask the visitor to wear sterile gloves into the hallway

questions.explanation: Both staff and visitors must use soap and water after contact with a C. difficile patient or their room environment because alcohol fails to inactivate bacterial spores.
questions.hint: Apply the spore-resistance rule to visitor education as well as nursing staff.
questions.subject: Hand Hygiene (WHO Standard)

questions.question: During WHO hand hygiene compliance auditing on a hospital ward, how is the Hand Hygiene Compliance Rate mathematically calculated?

options.text: (Number of soap bottles used / Number of beds) x 100
(Number of observed hand hygiene actions performed / Total number of observed hand hygiene opportunities) x 100
(Number of nurses on duty / Number of patients) x 100
(Number of HAI cases / Total admissions) x 100

questions.explanation: Under the WHO Direct Observation Tool, compliance percentage = (Actions performed / Opportunities observed) x 100.
questions.hint: Express compliance as the ratio of times hand hygiene was actually done out of all the times it was indicated.
questions.subject: Hand Hygiene (WHO Standard)

questions.question: A nurse develops painful cracks and weeping eczema on their hands due to frequent washing. Why is this an urgent infection control issue, and what should the nurse do?

options.text: Continue working normally with bare hands to let them air out

Damaged skin harbors higher bacterial counts (including S. aureus) and increases bloodborne exposure risk; apply approved hospital hand lotion, cover minor cuts with waterproof dressings, and consult occupational health
Switch to washing with hot water and household bleach
Use personal petroleum-based hand cream right before putting on latex gloves

questions.explanation: Intact skin is a primary barrier. Cracked skin colonizes heavily with pathogens. Only hospital-approved, glove-compatible lotions should be used (petroleum/oil-based lotions degrade latex gloves), and severe dermatitis requires occupational health evaluation.
questions.hint: Think about how broken skin alters bacterial colonization and why lotion compatibility with gloves matters.
questions.subject: Hand Hygiene (WHO Standard)

questions.question: Which WHO Hand Hygiene step specifically targets the tips of the fingers and areas beneath the fingernails?

options.text: Palm to palm
Right palm over left dorsum
Rotational rubbing of thumbs
Rotational rubbing, backwards and forwards, with clasped fingers of right hand in left palm (and vice versa)

questions.explanation: Step 6 of the WHO technique—rotating the bunched/clasped fingertips against the opposite palm—directly cleans the fingertips and subungual regions where bacterial counts are highest.
questions.hint: Visualize pressing your gathered fingertips into the center of your opposite palm in a circular motion.
questions.subject: Hand Hygiene (WHO Standard)

questions.question: A nurse checks a patient's bedside cardiac monitor alarm, silences it, and then walks directly to another patient's bedside to hand them a glass of water without performing hand hygiene. Which TWO WHO Moments were missed?

options.text: Moment 2 and Moment 3
Moment 5 (After touching Patient A's surroundings) and Moment 1 (Before touching Patient B)
Moment 3 and Moment 4
No moment was missed because the nurse did not touch Patient A's skin

questions.explanation: Touching Patient A's monitor triggers Moment 5 upon leaving Patient A's zone, and approaching Patient B triggers Moment 1 (which can be satisfied by a single properly timed hand hygiene action right between the two zones).
questions.hint: Identify the "environment" moment at Bed A and the "initial contact" moment at Bed B.
questions.subject: Hand Hygiene (WHO Standard)

questions.question:
Assertion (A): In WHO surgical hand preparation, using an alcohol-based surgical hand rub is considered an acceptable alternative to traditional antimicrobial soap-and-water scrubbing if hands are visibly clean.
Reason (R): Alcohol-based surgical hand rubs achieve equal or greater rapid microbial reduction with less skin irritation and water consumption than traditional brush scrubbing.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.explanation: WHO Global Guidelines for the Prevention of Surgical Site Infection explicitly endorse either antimicrobial soap-and-water scrub OR alcohol-based surgical hand rub (after an initial wash if soiled) as equally effective, noting superior skin tolerability with ABHR.
questions.hint: Recall WHO's modern stance on brushless alcohol-based surgical hand rubs versus traditional scrubbing.
questions.subject: Hand Hygiene (WHO Standard)

questions.question: Why does WHO advise AGAINST using stiff bristle scrub brushes on the skin of hands and forearms during surgical hand preparation?

options.text: Brushes are too expensive for hospitals
Stiff brushes cause micro-abrasions on the skin, increasing shedding of resident bacteria from deeper layers
Brushes dissolve chlorhexidine
Brushes take too little time

questions.explanation: Vigorous brushing abrades the epidermis and actually increases bacterial counts shed from damaged skin; WHO recommends using a soft sponge or brushless technique (using a nail cleaner only under fingernails if visibly dirty).
questions.hint: Think about what harsh bristles do to the surface of the epidermis and deeper resident bacteria.
questions.subject: Hand Hygiene (WHO Standard)

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a patient on Contact precautions for Norovirus gastroenteritis during a ward outbreak. Which hand hygiene agent is recommended by CDC/WHO?

options.text: Alcohol-based hand rub exclusively
Handwashing with soap and water (mechanical removal is preferred because non-enveloped norovirus has partial resistance to alcohol)
Dry wiping with a paper towel
Rinsing with cold water only without soap

questions.explanation: Norovirus is a non-enveloped virus that is relatively resistant to alcohol-based hand rubs. During norovirus outbreaks or direct care of symptomatic patients, soap and water handwashing is preferred.
questions.hint: Remember that besides bacterial spores, certain hardy non-enveloped GI outbreak viruses also require soap and water.
questions.subject: Hand Hygiene (WHO Standard)

questions.question: Which of the following statements about "Point-of-Care" hand hygiene in the WHO Multimodal Hand Hygiene Improvement Strategy is CORRECT?

options.text: Hand rub dispensers should be locked inside the nursing supervisor's office
Alcohol-based hand rub must be immediately accessible at the exact place where patient, healthcare worker, and care/treatment come together (e.g., bedside wall mount or pocket bottle)
Sinks should be placed only at the end of the hospital corridor
Hand hygiene is required only at the start and end of an 8-hour shift

questions.explanation: Point-of-care accessibility eliminates workflow barriers by placing ABHR within arm's reach of where care is delivered, which is a cornerstone of the WHO Multimodal Strategy.
questions.hint: Define "point of care" as the exact physical spot where nurse and patient interact.
questions.subject: Hand Hygiene (WHO Standard)

questions.question: A nurse is preparing to enter the room of a patient who has BOTH active pulmonary tuberculosis (Airborne) and a draining MRSA leg ulcer (Contact). Which PPE items must the nurse don, and in what exact order?

options.text: Gloves -> Gown -> N95 respirator
Gown -> N95 respirator -> Goggles/Face shield (if splash risk) -> Gloves
Surgical mask -> Gown -> Gloves
N95 respirator -> Gloves -> Gown

questions.explanation: Combining Airborne + Contact precautions requires Gown, N95 respirator, Eye protection (if splash risk), and Gloves—following the universal donning sequence: Gown -> Respirator -> Eye protection -> Gloves.
questions.hint: Combine the required PPE for both precautions and apply the standard body-to-face-to-hands donning order.
questions.subject: PPE Donning & Doffing

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a patient with COVID-19/SARS requiring Airborne + Contact + Eye protection. When using CDC's "Gown and Gloves Together" alternative doffing method, what is the FIRST step?

options.text: Pull off the N95 respirator first

Grasp the front of the gown at the waist/chest, pull away from the body to break ties gently, roll the gown inside-out into a bundle while simultaneously peeling off the gloves inside-out, then perform hand hygiene
Remove goggles with contaminated gloves first
Untie the neck strap while keeping gloves on

questions.explanation: CDC recognizes two safe doffing methods: (1) Gloves -> Goggles -> Gown -> Mask, OR (2) Gown and Gloves removed together in one controlled inside-out roll -> Hand hygiene -> Goggles -> Mask -> Hand hygiene.
questions.hint: Visualize rolling the gown downward from the front so the gloves peel off inside the bundle in one motion.
questions.subject: PPE Donning & Doffing

questions.question: While removing an N95 respirator outside a TB isolation room, the nurse touches ONLY the two elastic head straps. Which strap should be lifted off over the head FIRST?

options.text: The top strap first
The bottom strap first, followed by the top strap, lifting the respirator forward away from the face without touching the front filter surface
Both straps pulled forward by gripping the front cup
Snap the straps sharply against the cheeks

questions.explanation: Lifting the bottom elastic strap over the head first (while the top strap stabilizes the mask) and then lifting the top strap prevents the contaminated front of the N95 from swinging down onto the nurse's chest or uniform.
questions.hint: Apply the same bottom-first gravity rule used for tie-back surgical masks.
questions.subject: PPE Donning & Doffing

questions.question: A nurse is wearing goggles and a surgical mask while suctioning an open tracheostomy (high splash risk). After removing contaminated gloves, which surface of the goggles should the nurse grip to remove them?

options.text: The front clear plastic lens
The clean earpieces (temple arms) or back headband behind the ears
The bottom rim of the lens
Pull them off while still wearing bloody gloves

questions.explanation: The front lens of goggles/face shields is directly exposed to respiratory splashes and is heavily contaminated. Bare hands must grasp only the clean earpieces or rear headband to lift them forward and away from the face.
questions.hint: Touch only the parts resting behind the ears or head, never the shield facing the patient.
questions.subject: PPE Donning & Doffing

questions.question: During a hospital PPE audit, which actions by staff represent CRITICAL doffing errors that increase self-contamination? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Touching the front outer surface of a used surgical mask with bare fingers
Leaving a contaminated isolation gown hanging on a hook inside the hallway for reuse later
Removing an N95 mask inside an active TB patient's room before exiting
Performing hand hygiene immediately after removing all PPE

questions.explanation: Touching the mask front, reusing/hanging contaminated single-use isolation gowns in hallways, and removing an N95 inside an airborne room are severe contamination errors. Immediate post-doffing hand hygiene is mandatory and correct.
questions.hint: Spot the three breaches that expose bare skin, hallways, or lungs to pathogens.
questions.subject: PPE Donning & Doffing

questions.question: What is the difference between a Surgical Mask and an N95 Particulate Respirator?

options.text: Surgical masks filter 95% of airborne 0.3-micron particles tightly around the face

Surgical masks are loose-fitting barriers protecting against large droplets and splashes; N95 respirators are tight-fitting devices certified to filter at least 95% of very small airborne particles (0.3 microns)
N95 respirators are used only for Contact precautions
Surgical masks require annual quantitative fit-testing

questions.explanation: Surgical masks block large droplets/splashes and provide source control, but have loose side gaps. N95 respirators form a tight facial seal and filter >= 95% of 0.3-micron airborne aerosols (e.g., TB, measles, varicella).
questions.hint: Contrast loose-fitting droplet/splash protection with tight-sealing aerosol filtration.
questions.subject: PPE Donning & Doffing

questions.question: A nurse is preparing to insert a sterile urinary catheter for a female patient using a closed sterile kit. When putting on the SECOND sterile glove (with the dominant hand already sterilely gloved), where should the sterile gloved fingers be placed?

options.text: Touching the patient's thigh for balance
Slipped underneath the folded-back sterile outer cuff of the second glove (sterile-to-sterile) while keeping the thumb abducted away from the bare wrist
Gripping the inside skin-contact surface of the second glove
Pulling the second glove on with bare fingers

questions.explanation: Once the first hand is sterilely gloved, its sterile fingers slip under the folded cuff of the second glove (touching sterile exterior to sterile exterior) while keeping the sterile thumb angled away from the ungloved hand's skin.
questions.hint: Keep sterile surfaces touching only sterile surfaces and angle the thumb away from bare skin.
questions.subject: PPE Donning & Doffing

questions.question: When wearing a disposable isolation gown, how should the nurse fasten the gown to ensure complete back and front coverage?

options.text: Leave the neck and waist ties completely untied for quick removal
Cover the torso fully from neck to knees and arms to wrists, wrap around the back, and fasten both the neck and waist ties securely
Wear the gown backwards with the opening facing the patient
Tie the waist strings tightly around the front chest

questions.explanation: Proper donning covers the entire torso, wraps fully around the back, and secures both neck and waist ties so the gown does not gape open or dangle onto contaminated surfaces.
questions.hint: Think about how to keep the uniform completely covered without loose dangling edges.
questions.subject: PPE Donning & Doffing

questions.question: A nurse is assigned to care for a patient on Droplet precautions for Influenza. The nurse does NOT anticipate any blood/body fluid splashes or contact with draining wounds. Which single PPE item is MINIMUM required upon entering within 3 feet of the patient?

options.text: N95 respirator
Surgical mask (plus eye protection per facility respiratory-virus policy)
Sterile surgical gown
Shoe covers

questions.explanation: Droplet precautions specifically mandate wearing a surgical mask when entering the room or coming within 3 feet (1 meter) of the patient. Gloves/gown are added only if Standard Precautions (body fluid contact) apply.
questions.hint: Identify the core respiratory barrier required for large droplets within a 3-foot radius.
questions.subject: PPE Donning & Doffing

questions.question: A nurse completes a wound irrigation on a patient on Contact precautions and steps out into the corridor STILL wearing the contaminated gloves to grab a clean dressing roll from the supply cart. What infection control principle has been violated?

options.text: Airborne negative-pressure rule
Preventing environmental cross-contamination ("No gloves in hallways" / clean supply contamination)
Surgical hand scrubbing duration
Sterile field 1-inch border rule

questions.explanation: Wearing contaminated gloves outside an isolation room transfers pathogens directly onto doorknobs, clean supply carts, and shared computers. Gloves must ALWAYS be removed and hand hygiene performed before leaving the room or touching clean supplies.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to clean hallway supply carts when touched by dirty bedside gloves.
questions.subject: PPE Donning & Doffing

questions.question: When removing a soiled isolation gown inside a Contact precautions room, which technique prevents contaminating the nurse's uniform?

options.text: Pull the gown straight over the head like a T-shirt
Unfasten neck and waist ties, pull the gown away from the neck and shoulders touching ONLY the clean inside, turn it inside-out while folding/rolling into a compact bundle, and discard
Shake the gown vigorously to remove dust before discarding
Tuck the dirty front of the gown against your chest while walking to the bin

questions.explanation: Turning the gown inside-out while touching only the clean inner surfaces traps all external contamination inside the rolled bundle, preventing contact with the nurse's uniform or skin.
questions.hint: Picture rolling the dirty outer face inward so only the clean inner lining faces out.
questions.subject: PPE Donning & Doffing

questions.question: A nurse with a documented severe IgE-mediated latex allergy is preparing to perform a sterile urinary catheterization. Which PPE modification is mandatory?

options.text: Apply heavy moisturizing cream underneath standard latex gloves
Use latex-free (nitrile, neoprene, or polyisoprene) sterile gloves and ensure latex-free supplies
Wear powdered latex gloves for less than 5 minutes
Perform the procedure bare-handed to avoid allergy

questions.explanation: Powdered latex gloves aerosolize latex proteins and can trigger anaphylaxis in sensitized staff or patients. Non-latex synthetic sterile gloves (nitrile, neoprene, polyisoprene) provide safe barrier protection.
questions.hint: Choose the synthetic glove materials that completely eliminate natural rubber proteins.
questions.subject: PPE Donning & Doffing

questions.question: Which of the following situations require wearing EYE PROTECTION (goggles or full face shield) under Standard Precautions? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Assisting with endotracheal intubation or open airway suctioning
Irrigating a deep purulent abscess or arterial bleeding wound
Assisting with a vaginal delivery or cesarean section
Measuring an oral temperature on a calm, cooperative patient

questions.explanation: Standard Precautions require goggles or a face shield whenever there is a reasonable risk of splashes, sprays, or aerosols of blood, secretions, or body fluids reaching the eyes, nose, or mouth.
questions.hint: Identify the three procedures that carry a real risk of blood or fluid splashing toward the face.
questions.subject: PPE Donning & Doffing

questions.question: A nurse wears prescription eyeglasses and is about to perform an open tracheal suctioning on a coughing patient. Are regular prescription eyeglasses sufficient as PPE eye protection?

options.text: Yes, prescription lenses block all splashes completely
No; regular eyeglasses lack side shields and top/bottom coverage—the nurse must wear wrap-around goggles or a full face shield over them
Yes, if the nurse tilts their head slightly upward
No; the nurse must remove their prescription glasses and work without clear vision

questions.explanation: Standard personal eyeglasses do not provide splash protection from the sides, top, or bottom. Protective over-the-glasses goggles or a full-length face shield must be worn over prescription glasses.
questions.hint: Consider whether everyday spectacle frames seal off splashes coming from the sides or below.
questions.subject: PPE Donning & Doffing

questions.question: Why should a nurse NEVER pull a surgical mask down around their chin or neck between patients and then pull it back up over their nose?

options.text: It stretches the elastic ear loops slightly
The neck/chin area is contaminated, and pulling a contaminated mask up transfers pathogens directly onto the nurse's hands, nose, and mouth
It makes the mask warmer
It violates hospital dress-code colors only

questions.explanation: Once a mask is removed or lowered off the face, it must be discarded immediately (never worn around the neck or dangled from one ear) because touching the contaminated exterior and shifting it back up risks direct mucosal self-inoculation.
questions.hint: Think about how pathogens on the neck or outer mask surface reach the mouth and nose when a mask is repositioned.
questions.subject: PPE Donning & Doffing

questions.question: During a positive-pressure user seal check of an N95 respirator, the nurse places both hands gently over the respirator and exhales softly. What indicates a FAILED seal?

options.text: Slight positive pressure builds up inside the mask
Air leaks around the nose bridge (fogging glasses) or along the cheeks/chin edges
The straps rest smoothly at the crown and neck
No air escapes around the perimeter

questions.explanation: During a positive-pressure check, a proper seal causes slight pressure buildup inside the mask with NO air escaping around the edges. Fogging glasses or air blowing past the nose/cheeks indicates a failed seal requiring readjustment or a different size.
questions.hint: Notice the telltale physical sign (especially for eyeglass wearers) that exhaled air is escaping around the mask edges.
questions.subject: PPE Donning & Doffing

questions.question: In the Operating Theater, a scrub nurse who has already completed surgical hand antisepsis is donning a sterile surgical gown using closed gloving. Which statement is TRUE?

options.text: The scrub nurse touches the outside front of the gown with bare hands to pull it on
The scrub nurse grasps the inside neckline/shoulder area of the folded gown, slides arms into sleeves keeping hands INSIDE the sterile cuffs, while the circulating nurse fastens the back ties
The scrub nurse ties their own back neck ties with sterile gloved hands
The circulating nurse pulls the front sterile chest panel to straighten it

questions.explanation: In sterile gowning for closed gloving, the scrub nurse touches only the clean inside of the gown and keeps fingers inside the gown cuffs while the unsterile circulating nurse ties the back. Sterile gloves are then donned through the cuffs without bare skin ever touching the outside.
questions.hint: Separate the sterile inner/front handling by the scrub nurse from the unsterile back-tying done by the circulating nurse.
questions.subject: PPE Donning & Doffing

questions.question: A nurse is wearing a reusable heavy-duty face shield while working in an isolation unit. After doffing the face shield safely, what must be done before reusing it?

options.text: Wipe only the inside with a dry tissue
Clean and disinfect the face shield with an EPA-approved hospital disinfectant wipe/solution (following manufacturer contact time), rinse/dry, and store cleanly
Place it directly inside the nurse's scrub pocket
Autoclave the plastic shield at 134 C

questions.explanation: Reusable eye protection/face shields must be cleaned and disinfected with an approved hospital disinfectant (avoiding high-heat autoclaving that melts plastic) before storage and reuse.
questions.hint: Recall how reusable plastic eye shields are safely decontaminated without melting them.
questions.subject: PPE Donning & Doffing

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Hand hygiene is mandatory BOTH before donning PPE and immediately after doffing PPE.
Reason (R): Performing hand hygiene before donning prevents contaminating clean PPE and the patient, while hand hygiene after doffing removes any pathogens accidentally transferred onto the hands during removal.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.explanation: Pre-donning hand hygiene protects clean PPE and the patient from staff hand flora; post-doffing hand hygiene is the critical final safeguard against microscopic self-contamination during PPE removal.
questions.hint: Consider why clean hands matter both at the start of putting on clean barriers and at the end of taking off dirty ones.
questions.subject: PPE Donning & Doffing

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a patient on Contact precautions for MRSA. While inside the room, the nurse's glove tears while turning the patient. What is the nurse's immediate action?

options.text: Pull a second glove directly over the torn glove
Stop the task safely, remove both gloves using safe doffing technique, perform hand hygiene immediately, and don a fresh pair of clean gloves
Finish turning the patient and wash hands 10 minutes later
Tape the tear closed with micropore tape

questions.explanation: Whenever a glove tears during patient care, remove it promptly, perform hand hygiene to remove any contamination that reached the skin, and put on fresh gloves before resuming care.
questions.hint: Never layer a new glove over a torn dirty one—clean the skin first before re-gloving.
questions.subject: PPE Donning & Doffing

questions.question: Which chemical sterilization/high-level disinfection agent is increasingly used as a faster, less irritating alternative to 2% glutaraldehyde for flexible endoscopes, requiring only 12 minutes at 20 C for high-level disinfection?

options.text: 70% Ethanol
0.55% Ortho-phthalaldehyde (OPA)
0.1% Sodium hypochlorite
Cetrimide

questions.explanation: Ortho-phthalaldehyde (0.55% OPA / Cidex OPA) requires no activation, has superior mycobactericidal activity, achieves HLD in 12 minutes at room temperature (vs 20–45 min for glutaraldehyde), and produces fewer irritating fumes—though it stains proteins/skin gray and is contraindicated for cystoscopes in bladder cancer patients due to rare anaphylaxis.
questions.hint: Think of the aldehyde cousin of glutaraldehyde known for a 12-minute HLD time and no activation requirement.
questions.subject: Sterilization, Disinfection & CSSD

questions.question: In CSSD sterilization monitoring, what are the THREE main categories of indicators used to validate every sterilization process?

options.text: Visual, olfactory, and auditory indicators
Mechanical (physical gauges/printouts), Chemical (Class 1–6 strips/tapes), and Biological (bacterial spore tests) indicators
Financial, administrative, and clinical indicators
Temperature, humidity, and weight indicators only

questions.explanation: Comprehensive CSSD quality assurance combines Mechanical/Physical monitoring (time, temperature, pressure charts per cycle), Chemical indicators (external tape + internal integrators per pack), and Biological indicators (spore vials—the ONLY direct proof of actual microbial kill).
questions.hint: Recall the triad of machine-gauge checks, color-changing strips, and live bacterial spore tests.
questions.subject: Sterilization, Disinfection & CSSD

questions.question: A surgical instrument pack removed from a steam autoclave shows dark diagonal stripes on the external autoclave tape (Class 1 chemical indicator). What does this color change prove?

options.text: The instruments inside the center of the pack are 100% sterile
Only that the outside of the pack was exposed to heat/steam (distinguishing processed from unprocessed packs), NOT guaranteed internal sterility
That all bacterial spores inside the chamber were destroyed
That the pack can be stored safely for 10 years

questions.explanation: Class 1 process indicators (autoclave tape) ONLY confirm that a pack passed through a sterilizer cycle; they do not verify steam penetration or spore kill. Internal Class 5 integrators and Biological spore indicators confirm true sterilization efficacy.
questions.hint: Separate external "exposure confirmation" from proof that steam penetrated the center and killed spores.
questions.subject: Sterilization, Disinfection & CSSD

questions.question: Which biological indicator organism is used to test the efficacy of a Hot Air Oven (dry heat) and an Ethylene Oxide (ETO) gas sterilizer?

options.text: Geobacillus stearothermophilus
Bacillus atrophaeus (formerly Bacillus subtilis var. niger)
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Mycobacterium tuberculosis

questions.explanation: [AIIMS NORCET PYQ] Bacillus atrophaeus spores are specifically resistant to dry heat and ethylene oxide gas, making them the standard biological indicator for Hot Air Ovens and ETO sterilizers (whereas Geobacillus stearothermophilus is used for steam autoclaves and H2O2 plasma).
questions.hint: Recall the Bacillus species paired with dry heat and ETO gas (as opposed to the thermophilic Geobacillus used for steam).
questions.subject: Sterilization, Disinfection & CSSD

questions.question: What is the key advantage of Hydrogen Peroxide Gas Plasma (STERRAD) sterilization over Ethylene Oxide (ETO) gas sterilization in a modern CSSD?

options.text: It works on large stacks of linen and absorbent cellulose paper
Short cycle time (45–75 minutes), no toxic chemical residues (byproducts are water vapor and oxygen), and NO prolonged aeration period required
It is much hotter than a steam autoclave (180 C)
It uses liquid bleach inside the chamber

questions.explanation: Hydrogen peroxide gas plasma sterilizes heat- and moisture-sensitive instruments at low temperature (~45–50 C) in under an hour, breaking down into harmless water and oxygen with zero aeration delay. However, it cannot penetrate cellulose/paper/linen or very long narrow lumens.
questions.hint: Focus on cycle speed, harmless byproducts (water + oxygen), and elimination of 12-hour aeration.
questions.subject: Sterilization, Disinfection & CSSD

questions.question: In CSSD, why must soiled surgical instruments be thoroughly cleaned (manually or in an ultrasonic washer/washer-disinfector) BEFORE being placed into an autoclave or chemical sterilant?

options.text: Cleaning makes instruments heavier
Organic matter (dried blood, pus, tissue) physically shields microorganisms from steam/chemicals and inactivates certain chemical disinfectants
Cleaning replaces the need for sterilization
Autoclaves cannot turn on unless instruments are wet

questions.explanation: "You can clean without sterilizing, but you can NEVER sterilize without cleaning first." Residual blood, mucus, or bioburden blocks steam/chemical penetration and neutralizes disinfectants like chlorine and glutaraldehyde.
questions.hint: Think about what dried blood or tissue does when it coats bacteria inside a sterilizer.
questions.subject: Sterilization, Disinfection & CSSD

questions.question: What air-pressure gradient must be maintained across the THREE core zones of a standard CSSD?

options.text: Positive pressure in Decontamination; Negative pressure in Sterile Storage
Negative pressure in Decontamination (Dirty zone); Positive pressure in Assembly/Packaging (Clean zone) and Sterile Storage zone
Negative pressure in all three zones
Equal uncontrolled airflow with open windows

questions.explanation: Maintaining negative pressure in the Dirty/Decontamination zone traps aerosols and dirty air from escaping, while positive pressure in the Clean and Sterile Storage zones pushes clean filtered air outward to prevent dust/microbes from entering sterile storage.
questions.hint: Match negative pressure to trapping dirty aerosols and positive pressure to keeping sterile packs dust-free.
questions.subject: Sterilization, Disinfection & CSSD

questions.question: Which sterilization method is used commercially for pre-packaged disposable syringes, suture materials, IV cannulas, and surgical gloves?

options.text: Boiling for 10 minutes
Ionizing radiation (Gamma rays from Cobalt-60 or Electron beam) — "Cold Sterilization"
Hot air oven at 160 C
70% Alcohol immersion

questions.explanation: [AIIMS NORCET PYQ] Gamma radiation (Cobalt-60) is called "cold sterilization" because it penetrates sealed heat-sensitive plastic packages (disposable syringes, cannulas, sutures, catheters) and destroys microbial DNA without raising temperature.
questions.hint: Recall the industrial "cold sterilization" method that penetrates sealed disposable plastic medical supplies.
questions.subject: Sterilization, Disinfection & CSSD

questions.question: How long must a heat-sensitive semi-critical instrument (e.g., endoscope) be immersed in 2% alkaline glutaraldehyde (Cidex) to achieve High-Level Disinfection (HLD) versus full Chemical Sterilization (sporicidal)?

options.text: 2 minutes for HLD; 10 minutes for Sterilization
20–45 minutes for HLD; 10 hours for complete Sterilization
10 hours for HLD; 20 minutes for Sterilization
5 minutes for both HLD and Sterilization

questions.explanation: [AIIMS NORCET PYQ] In 2% alkaline glutaraldehyde (Cidex), vegetative microbes, viruses, and mycobacteria are killed in 20–45 minutes (HLD), whereas destroying hardy bacterial spores (full sterilization) requires 10 hours of continuous immersion.
questions.hint: Remember the sharp jump from less than an hour for HLD to a double-digit hour soak for killing spores.
questions.subject: Sterilization, Disinfection & CSSD

questions.question: Which Spaulding classification category and processing level apply to laryngoscope blades, endotracheal tubes, respiratory therapy circuits, and vaginal specula?

options.text: Critical; sterilization only
Semi-critical; High-Level Disinfection (HLD) at minimum (or sterilization when heat-stable)
Non-critical; low-level disinfection
Non-critical; soap and water only

questions.explanation: Semi-critical items contact intact mucous membranes or non-intact skin (endoscopes, laryngoscope blades, ETTs, anesthesia circuits, specula) and require at minimum High-Level Disinfection (or sterilization if heat-tolerant).
questions.hint: Notice that all listed items touch mucous membranes without piercing sterile body cavities or bloodstreams.
questions.subject: Sterilization, Disinfection & CSSD

questions.question: Which of the following statements about "Flash Sterilization" (Immediate-Use Steam Sterilization — IUSS) are TRUE? (Select all that apply)

options.text: It uses an unwrapped high-temperature cycle (typically 132–134 C at ~30 psi for 3–4 minutes)
It is reserved strictly for emergencies (e.g., an irreplaceable surgical instrument dropped on the OT floor during surgery)
It should be used routinely as a shortcut to replace standard CSSD inventory
Instruments must still be thoroughly cleaned before IUSS and transferred aseptically for immediate use without storage

questions.explanation: IUSS (flash sterilization) runs at 132–134 C for 3–4 minutes for unwrapped items in emergencies only—never as a routine substitute for adequate instrument sets—and still requires pre-cleaning and immediate use.
questions.hint: Separate emergency unwrapped rapid steam parameters from improper routine shortcuts.
questions.subject: Sterilization, Disinfection & CSSD

questions.question: What is the correct concentration of freshly prepared Sodium Hypochlorite used for disinfecting a SMALL blood spill (< 10 mL) versus a LARGE blood spill (> 10 mL) per standard hospital infection control protocols?

options.text: 0.01% for both small and large spills
0.5% (5,000 ppm) for small spills / routine surface disinfection; 1% (10,000 ppm) for large blood spills
10% concentrated bleach directly on all surfaces
70% alcohol for large blood spills

questions.explanation: Standard Indian/AIIMS/NACO spill protocols recommend 0.5% (5,000 ppm) sodium hypochlorite for small blood spots (< 10 mL) and 1% (10,000 ppm) for large blood spills (> 10 mL, covered with absorbent material first, contact time 10–20 minutes).
questions.hint: Remember that larger volumes of organic blood require double the chlorine concentration (10,000 ppm vs 5,000 ppm).
questions.subject: Sterilization, Disinfection & CSSD

questions.question: Why is Ethyl Alcohol (70%) NOT recommended as a high-level disinfectant for sterilizing surgical instruments or large blood spills?

options.text: It is too expensive
It is NOT sporicidal, evaporates too rapidly, is inactivated by organic matter (blood), and can damage lens cement on endoscopes
It cannot kill Gram-positive bacteria
It leaves a thick oily residue

questions.explanation: Alcohol (60–80%) is an intermediate-level disinfectant ideal for small clean surfaces (vial tops, stethoscopes, thermometers) but lacks sporicidal activity, penetrates organic blood poorly, and hardens rubber/lens adhesives.
questions.hint: Think about alcohol's inability to kill spores and its rapid evaporation in the presence of blood.
questions.subject: Sterilization, Disinfection & CSSD

questions.question: Which type of chemical indicator (ISO 11140) is placed INSIDE every surgical tray/pack to react to ALL critical sterilization parameters (time, temperature, and steam saturation) and most closely parallels biological spore kill?

options.text: Class 1 (Process indicator / external tape)
Class 2 (Bowie-Dick test)
Class 5 (Integrating indicator / Integrator)
Visual moisture gauge only

questions.explanation: Class 5 Integrating Indicators (integrators) respond to all critical variables (time, temperature, moisture/steam) across a defined performance curve matched to Geobacillus stearothermophilus spore inactivation.
questions.hint: Identify the internal strip class known as an "integrator" because it tracks every critical cycle variable together.
questions.subject: Sterilization, Disinfection & CSSD

questions.question: A patient with suspected Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD — a prion disease) undergoes a neurosurgical brain biopsy. Why are standard autoclave cycles (121 C for 15 minutes) inadequate for these surgical instruments?

options.text: Prions are large fungi that resist pressure

Prions are abnormally folded proteins extremely resistant to routine steam sterilization, alcohol, and formalin; single-use disposable instruments (incinerated) or specialized extended NaOH + 134 C protocols are required
Prions dissolve stainless steel
Prions are killed easily by plain soap

questions.explanation: Prions lack nucleic acids and survive routine autoclaving, UV, alcohol, and aldehydes. High-risk CNS/ocular tissue instruments from CJD patients should be single-use and incinerated, or subjected to strict WHO prion protocols (1N NaOH immersion + prolonged 134 C prevacuum autoclaving).
questions.hint: Recall that infectious misfolded proteins survive normal autoclave times and require disposable incineration or harsh alkali + extended 134 C cycles.
questions.subject: Sterilization, Disinfection & CSSD

questions.question: What is the standard method of "Pasteurization" (Holder method vs Flash method) used for milk and heat-sensitive respiratory therapy equipment?

options.text: 121 C for 15 minutes
Holder method: 63 C for 30 minutes; Flash method: 72 C for 15–20 seconds (followed by rapid cooling)
160 C for 2 hours
100 C for 60 minutes

questions.explanation: Pasteurization eliminates non-spore-forming pathogens (like M. tuberculosis, Brucella, Salmonella) using moist heat below boiling: Holder method (63 C for 30 min) or Flash/HTST method (72 C for 15–20 sec).
questions.hint: Match the two classic sub-boiling milk-safety temperatures (63 C and 72 C) with their durations.
questions.subject: Sterilization, Disinfection & CSSD

questions.question: In CSSD sterile storage, how far off the floor, below the ceiling/sprinkler heads, and away from outside walls must sterile supply shelves be positioned?

options.text: Directly on the floor to maximize shelf space
At least 8–10 inches (20–25 cm) above the floor, 18 inches (45 cm) below ceiling/sprinkler heads, and 2 inches (5 cm) from exterior walls
1 inch above the floor and touching the ceiling
Distance from floor and ceiling does not matter in CSSD

questions.explanation: Elevating bottom shelves 8–10 inches prevents floor-cleaning moisture/dust contamination; 18-inch ceiling clearance ensures fire-sprinkler coverage and airflow; 2-inch wall clearance prevents condensation moisture from exterior walls.
questions.hint: Recall the standard 8–10 inch floor clearance and 18-inch sprinkler-head clearance rule.
questions.subject: Sterilization, Disinfection & CSSD

questions.question: Which method of sterilization uses "Tyndallization" (intermittent steaming at 100 C for 20 minutes on 3 consecutive days)?

options.text: Metal surgical scalpels
Heat-sensitive culture media containing sugars, gelatin, or egg (e.g., Lowenstein-Jensen medium) that would be damaged above 100 C
Silicone Foley catheters
Orthopedic titanium implants

questions.explanation: Tyndallization (fractional sterilization) steams delicate sugar/egg/gelatin media at 100 C for 20 min on 3 successive days: Day 1 kills vegetative cells; overnight incubation lets spores germinate; Days 2 and 3 kill the newly germinated cells.
questions.hint: Connect the 3-day intermittent 100 C steaming technique to delicate microbiology culture media.
questions.subject: Sterilization, Disinfection & CSSD

questions.question: A nurse cleans a glass mercury/digital oral thermometer between uses on the same patient, or a shared thermometer with a disposable sheath. Which Spaulding category applies to a reusable oral/rectal thermometer without a sheath?

options.text: Critical item
Semi-critical item (contacts oral/rectal mucous membranes; requires high-level or intermediate-level disinfection such as 70% alcohol per protocol)
Non-critical item contacting intact skin only
General municipal item

questions.explanation: Thermometers contacting oral or rectal mucosa are classified as semi-critical (or at minimum require intermediate-level disinfection like 70% alcohol / dedicated patient use + probe covers to prevent cross-transmission of C. diff/VRE).
questions.hint: Consider which body surface an oral or rectal probe directly touches.
questions.subject: Sterilization, Disinfection & CSSD

questions.question: Which of the following items are INCOMPATIBLE with steam autoclaving in CSSD? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Flexible fiberoptic colonoscopes
Anhydrous petroleum jelly (Vaseline) and talcum powders
Delicate plastic single-use IV catheters

Followed by shredding or mutilation (to prevent illegal reuse)
